name: Persian, Iranian
catalog_quote: Word stress falls on the final syllable of nouns and pronouns. ..neither the indefinite or the definite article (-i -ra) carries stress (these are affixed to the end of the noun stem).. (Lambton 1953:7)
sweep_summary: Persian (west2369, catalog fixed-strict final; deciding quote Lambton 1953:7 via StressTyp2, audit CSV names Amini 1997). Of the 10 sweep items, 5 were obtained and read in full: Hosseini 2014 (UTokyo dissertation, 209 pp., open repository) is the best new first-hand statement — final stress in nouns/adjectives/verb roots/most adverbs and in compounds and derivations, inflectional suffixes stressless except -hâ/-ân, -tar/-tarin, -e, verb prefixes prominent, Arabic-loan particles initially stressed — confirming the final coding and refining its edges; Modarresi 2014 (HU Berlin dissertation) is sentence-level prosody and silent on word stress; the two Taheri-Ardali Speech Prosody focus papers (2012, 2014) are silent on placement. A bonus open paper found on the same ISCA index, Abolhasanizadeh 2012 (SP 2012), states 'Final syllables of nouns, adjectives, most adverbs and unprefixed verbs have the stress. Prefixed verbs take stress on the prefix' and shows f0 alone cues the location. Paywalled and not read: Ferguson 1957 (abstract obtained: stress contrastive, máhi vs mahí; priority high), Kahnemuyipour 2003 NLLT (summarised by Hosseini; open 2000 precursor already held; medium) and Abolhasanizadeh et al. 2012 Lingua (summarised by Hosseini and its SP companion; medium). Not found: Mahjani 2003 (Edinburgh MSc, intonation) and Eslami 2000 (Tehran PhD, Persian, sentence prosody), both low priority. Falahati 2020 is L2-acquisition, not relevant. everything came from repository APIs, ISCA archive, Crossref and curl. All fetched sources

new_statements.quote: In nouns, adjectives, verb roots and most adverbs, the rightmost syllable is metrically strong (stressed). Every lexical word in Persian has one and only one stressed syllable and the place of stress does not depend on the weight or the number of syllables ... even in long words containing heavy syllables, only the rightmost syllable is stressed. ... Compound nouns and adjectives as well, have only one stress on the last syllable of the compound, regardless of the word length. ... Inflectional suffixes on the other hand, fall out of the stress domain and are always stressless.
new_statements.citation: Hosseini, Seyed Ayat (2014). The phonology and phonetics of prosodic prominence in Persian. Doctoral dissertation, University of Tokyo (repository record 6575, file; hdl 2261/57678; doi 10.15083/00006566).
new_statements.reading: Fixed final stress on the lexical word (nouns, adjectives, verb roots, most adverbs; compounds and derivations included), weight- and length-insensitive, with inflectional suffixes and clitics outside the domain — this confirms the catalog's final-syllable coding for nouns. The same pages refine it: the plural -hâ/-ân, comparative/superlative -tar/-tarin and perfective -e DO attract stress (pedar-hấ, bad-tár, mord-é), conjugated verbs are prominent on the leftmost prefix (mí-xând-am), and a closed set of (mostly Arabic-loan) discourse particles is initially stressed (§3.7, p. 60). Together with the earlier-held Rahmani/Gussenhoven line, Hosseini treats the prominence as a single edgemost 'stress' realised as a pitch accent. Nothing read contradicts 'final' as the dominant pattern; the strict=true register remains the point of caution (verb prefixes, particles).

(1) Hosseini is not merely 'together with the Rahmani/Gussenhoven line': he explicitly classifies Persian as a 'prototypical stress language' on Hyman's canonical-stress criteria (Table 2, printed p. 12 / PDF p. 23: 'Word stress is always rightmost (final)', 'Stress is weight-insensitive', 'There are no secondary stresses at word level') and keeps abstract metrical strength (right-aligned iambic foot head, §3.2 p. 26; §4.6 pp. 97-98) distinct from the pitch accent that docks on it — a stronger match for the catalog's fixed-strict, domain=WORD, rule 01/…

audit.action: cite a better source for the same coding
audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed-strict, final syllable' rests on Amini 1997 (TWPL phonology paper), whose three deciding passages are verbatim in the held scanned at the stated pages (1, 2, 4). Two held dissertations (Sadat-Tehrani 2007 p. 22; Rohany Rahbar 2012) and four open sources fetched sources now (Kahnemuyipour 2000 ZASPiL pp. 120/122; Rahmani et al. 2015 PLoS ONE p. 4; Rahmani et al. 2016; Rahmani 2018) all state that nouns/adjectives, simple, derived or compound, carry prominence on the final syllable, clitics excluded; prefixed verbs take prefix stress. No source contradicts the position. The refinement worth a caution note, not a recode: Rahmani, Rietveld & Gussenhoven (2015-2018) argue the final prominence is a post-lexical f0 accent (Persian listeners are stress-'deaf'), i.e. the language may lack lexical stress proper while the surface rule stays right-edge. sources.citation: Hosseini, Seyed Ayat (2014). The phonology and phonetics of prosodic prominence in Persian. Doctoral dissertation, University of Tokyo. 209 pp.
sources.quote: In nouns, adjectives, verb roots and most adverbs, the rightmost syllable is metrically strong (stressed). Every lexical word in Persian has one and only one stressed syllable and the place of stress does not depend on the weight or the number of syllables ... Compound nouns and adjectives as well, have only one stress on the last syllable of the compound, regardless of the word length. ... Derivational affixation is very similar to compounding, in that the stress falls on the last syllable of the whole affixed word. ... Inflectional suffixes on the other hand, fall out of the stress domain and are always stressless. (pp. 10-11)

sources.citation: Rahmani, Hamed. 2018. Persian 'word stress' is a syntax-driven tone. Proc. 6th International Symposium on Tonal Aspects of Languages (TAL 2018), Berlin. doi:10.21437/TAL.2018-31
sources.quote: 'Nouns and adjectives, whether simple, derived or compound, are stressed on the final syllable without exception. Unprefixed verbs have stress on the final syllable of the stem, while prefixed verbs are stressed on the leftmost prefix.' Argues the prominence is an f0 H tone/accent assigned by syntax, not lexical stress.

sources.citation: Rahmani, Hamed, Toni Rietveld & Carlos Gussenhoven. 2016. Persian word accent is deletable. Proc. Speech Prosody 2016, Boston. doi:10.21437/SpeechProsody.2016-90
sources.quote: Accent assigned 'to the final syllable of morphological words, skipping' clitics; production + perception experiments show the word accent is deleted post-focally and in presupposed clauses.

sources.citation: Rahmani, Hamed, Toni Rietveld & Carlos Gussenhoven. 2015. Stress "deafness" reveals absence of lexical marking of stress or tone in the adult grammar. PLoS ONE 10(12): e0143968. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0143968
sources.quote: 'Morphological words, whether simple, derivationally complex or compound, are accented on the final syllable. However, prosodically deficient morphemes [clitics] are integrated into a phonological word with a morphological host to their left' ... 'We refer to the Persian post-lexical prominence as accent, because its stress does not involve any phonetic cues, like durational and spectral features, other than f0'. Persian listeners pattern as stress-'deaf' (perception experiment).

sources.citation: Abolhasanizadeh, Vahideh (2012). F0 as the dominant cue to accent location in Persian. Proc. Speech Prosody 2012 (Shanghai). [EXTRA: not in the sweep list; found on the same ISCA index page; open companion of the Lingua 2012 paper, work with Gussenhoven & Bijankhan]
sources.quote: Stress assignment is straightforward. Final syllables of nouns, adjectives, most adverbs and unprefixed verbs have the stress [8, 10]. Prefixed verbs take stress on the prefix. ... Persian presents minimal stress pairs because clitics are not included in the domain for stress assignment, which attracts a stress on the last syllable.
sources.note: Final stress in nouns, adjectives, most adverbs and unprefixed verbs; prefix stress in prefixed verbs; clitics outside the stress domain (tâbeš 'light' vs tâb-eš 'his toy'). Two categorical-perception experiments show f0 alone switches the word vs word+clitic judgement 100%, i.e. the prominence 'earlier known as stress' is a pitch accent.

sources.citation: Kahnemuyipour, Arsalan. 2000. The word is a phrase, phonologically: evidence from Persian stress. ZAS Papers in Linguistics 19: 119-136. doi:10.21248/zaspil.19.2000.70
sources.quote: p. 120: 'Some examples of simple nouns and adjectives are given in (2). The stress is word-final.' p. 122: 'Word stress rule: The final syllable in the (phonological) word takes stress (End Rule Right).' Prefixed verbs get initial (prefix) stress via a separate phrase-level rule (leftmost phonological word); fn. 13 notes a handful of lexical exceptions.

sources.quote: 'ez' stands for Ezafe, which is a type of linker indicated by an unstressed vowel -e (-ye after vowels) which appears between a noun and its subsequent adjective (p. 17 n. 7)
sources.locator: whole text searched; ch. 3 'Prosody and the interpretation of objects' (p. 132ff.) and ch. 4 'Prosody and the interpretation of subjects'; p. 17 n. 7
sources.note: A semantics/syntax dissertation on bare nouns; its 'prosody' is sentence-level nuclear accent placement under information structure (accent marked by boldface on whole words). It never states where word stress falls; the only word-level remark is that the Ezafe vowel is unstressed.

sources.citation: Taheri-Ardali, Mortaza, Hamed Rahmani & Yi Xu (2014). The perception of prosodic focus in Persian. Proc. Speech Prosody 2014 (Dublin), 515-519.
sources.quote: Persian has traditionally been described as a stress language. Abolhasanizade et al [1] recently found no marked phonetic difference between stressed and unstressed syllables independently of the presence of intonational pitch accents. The authors conclude that Persian word prosody involves a lexically-sensitive pitch accent assignment system that is more like Tokyo Japanese, which has no stress in the phonetic sense, than West Germanic (p. 515)
sources.note: A focus-perception experiment (post-focus compression). It does not state where word stress falls; it only relays the pitch-accent (non-stress) interpretation of Persian word prominence.

sources.note: Acoustic study of focus (F0, duration, intensity before/on/after focus; Persian is a post-focus-compression language). No statement on word-stress placement.
